1170.bp: When you ask a search engine a complex, multi-sentence question like 'What are the environmental impacts of hydroelectric dams in Southeast Asia and how do they compare to solar farming?', you want relevant papers—but the system needs a reliable, predictable way to rank them. This matters because reasoning-heavy questions are becoming normal as AI assistants help with complex research, yet most search tools were built for short keyword queries like 'hydroelectric dam impacts'.
1170.wh: The problem: if you simply feed a long, complex query into BM25 (a 50-year-old text-matching baseline), it treats each word equally and gets overwhelmed by length and detail. The naive version of BM25 doesn't know how to emphasize the important parts of your multi-part question versus the filler words, so it struggles to find truly relevant papers.
1170.ap: The researchers found that BM25Q—a variant that flips the weighting logic—works much better on long questions. Instead of just weighing the question itself as raw text, BM25Q applies BM25's statistical importance-scoring to the question terms first, essentially identifying which parts of your question are the distinctive keywords before matching against papers. They then tested this across five additional datasets to see if the trick was universal.
1170.ww: When you ask a long question, most of the words are ordinary (and, the, for), while a few words actually carry the meaning (hydroelectric, dam, environmental impact). BM25Q finds those meaningful words automatically and says 'these are the query words that actually matter', leading to better matches. The weighting mimics how humans instinctively identify the core ideas in a long sentence.
1170.po: On the BRIGHT benchmark (a dataset of complex reasoning-focused questions), BM25Q consistently beats standard BM25. However, the authors discovered that BM25Q's gains don't transfer reliably to other datasets, whereas blending BM25Q with standard BM25 gives steady improvements everywhere. This means the strongest baseline for long-query search is not a single trick but a mixture of approaches.

1171.bp: A conversational search agent—think of a chatbot that remembers what you asked earlier and adapts its answers to your preferences—is far more useful than a one-shot search engine. Building such systems requires rich real-world test data with actual conversations, user profiles, and the messy ground truth of what humans actually want.
1171.wh: The obstacle: most public datasets have only short, isolated conversations. Real users ask questions across multiple sessions over days or weeks, refining their needs and switching contexts. Also, measuring whether a personalized response is 'better' is subjective and expensive—you need human judges who understand the context deeply. Without datasets like this, researchers can only guess.
1171.ap: TREC iKAT 2025 collected complex information needs and long, multi-session conversations (many dialogues per user) with manually designed user profiles and dynamically evolving user models. The collection includes both human-written conversations and interactions between automated systems and realistic user simulators. Every response was judged by humans at scale to provide ground-truth labels.
1171.ww: To build personalization that actually works, you must see how users' preferences shift over time within a single interaction and across separate sessions days apart. Without that longitudinal pattern, any personalization system will fail to capture the real challenge: recognizing when a user's intent has genuinely shifted versus when they're just refining an earlier question. The multi-session, human-judged format exposes these patterns.
1171.po: The iKAT 2025 collection provides researchers with 1000+ conversations spanning multiple turns per user, real user profiles, simulated user models, and large-scale human assessments. This publicly available resource enables reproducible research on conversational personalization—the next frontier in search—rather than ad-hoc lab prototypes.

1172.bp: Scientists publish papers filled with jargon, statistical details, and specialist assumptions—which means ordinary people cannot access crucial health and safety information. If we could automatically simplify biomedical abstracts into plain language, patients, families, and informed citizens could make better decisions about treatments, vaccines, and health policy.
1172.wh: The hard part: simplification is not just about swapping hard words for easy ones. Scientific language uses complex grammar, nested ideas, and implicit assumptions about what the reader already knows. A good simplification must preserve the actual meaning and nuance while using simpler words and shorter sentences, and it must work at the document level—explaining how one finding connects to the next—not just tweaking individual sentences.
1172.ap: BioCLEAR is a benchmark combining Cochrane systematic reviews with plain-language summaries written by humans, aligned at both the document and sentence level. It includes abstracts, their plain-language versions, sentence-level simplifications from other datasets, and submissions from dozens of AI systems tried on the task. This lets researchers see what works and what doesn't.
1172.ww: By providing aligned pairs—original abstract next to a plain-language version—researchers can train and test systems to recognize what *good* simplification looks like. The document-level aspect is crucial: a reader needs to understand not just individual sentences but how findings flow together, which is why this benchmark captures discourse structure (the logical flow) that simpler, sentence-by-sentence datasets miss.
1172.po: BioCLEAR enables systematic measurement of simplification quality across AI models, revealing which approaches preserve meaning and which collapse nuance. It also surfaces what current models still struggle with—likely subtle concepts and domain-specific reasoning—guiding future research in making science accessible.

1173.bp: Lawyers, judges, and citizens need to find relevant court decisions to argue a case or understand precedent. In many countries (especially those with civil law systems like Korea), there are no centralized citation networks showing which cases reference which others. Building a reliable search tool for legal documents is crucial for justice and efficiency, yet the technical and legal challenges are formidable.
1173.wh: The barrier: law is jurisdiction-specific, and what makes two cases 'relevant' involves both factual similarity (did both involve a breach of contract?) and legal reasoning (did the judge cite the same legal principle?). In common-law countries, judges cite precedents explicitly, so search tools can follow citation chains. In statutory-law countries like Korea, cases do not cite each other as much, making relevance judgments purely based on semantic and conceptual matching—far harder to learn from.
1173.ap: KCC provides 2,942 query–case pairs from 38,372 real Korean court decisions, each pair hand-labeled by legal experts with a four-level relevance rating (e.g., 'highly relevant', 'marginally relevant'). The labeling process captures both factual similarity and legal reasoning. The authors also published their annotation guide so other countries can adapt it to their own legal systems.
1173.ww: Expert-validated labels are essential because laypeople cannot reliably judge whether two legal cases are truly analogous. The four-level scale reveals that relevance is not binary; some cases are partially relevant (worth reading but not directly applicable). Training systems on these nuanced labels teaches them to recognize the patterns in legal reasoning—what makes a case truly on point.
1173.po: Researchers can now benchmark legal search systems—traditional text matching, neural rankers, and LLM-based methods—on a Korean-language dataset with expert ground truth. This opens the door to improving legal access in civil-law jurisdictions and provides a reusable framework for building similar benchmarks in other countries with different legal traditions.

1174.bp: Open-source software is built by millions of people collaborating across organizations. Understanding how code flows between teams, which organizations lead innovation, and how security vulnerabilities spread through dependency networks is crucial for building faster, safer software. But most research looks at individual projects in isolation.
1174.wh: The challenge: individual GitHub repositories are separate islands. To understand large-scale patterns—how one organization's innovation spreads to others, or how a security flaw affects the whole ecosystem—you need to see the full graph of who uses whose code and how. This requires massive data collection and careful handling of the social and technical layers simultaneously.
1174.ap: GONets maps over 230,000 GitHub organizations, 2.5 million users, and 4.3 million repositories as a bipartite network (users on one side, repos on the other, with edges showing contributions). The dataset includes detailed organizational metadata—size, creation date, follower count—and the pipeline automatically collects this information via GitHub's public API, then aggregates contribution patterns.
1174.ww: A bipartite network reveals asymmetries: some organizations maintain many repositories with many contributors; others are single-person shops. By mapping contributions at the organizational level rather than project level, researchers can see patterns invisible in traditional studies—how innovation spreads between organizations, which teams act as gateways, and where security risks concentrate.
1174.po: Researchers can now study how code reuse patterns evolve, trace collaboration dynamics between teams, and map the security ecosystem of GitHub organizations. The released dataset and collection pipeline enable reproducible, large-scale studies on open-source governance and risk—questions that were previously unanswerable.

1175.bp: Millions of people speak African languages and dialects, yet machine learning systems almost never work well for them. Building search tools that work in Ehugbo (the Afikpo dialect of Igbo, spoken by 150,000 people in Nigeria) seems like a technical problem, but it exposes a deeper design flaw in multilingual AI.
1175.wh: The intuitive assumption: if you build a machine learning model on diverse African language data, it should perform well on any African language. But the paper reveals a shocking finding: African-focused models trained on Igbo actually fail at retrieving relevant documents in Ehugbo (under 5% accuracy), while global models trained on many unrelated languages succeed (85% accuracy). Why? Knowing the language is not the same as bridging it to other languages.
1175.ap: The researchers created an evaluation benchmark from Ehugbo Bible audio (1 hour) aligned with English translations, giving a clean parallel corpus for testing. They tested African-centric models (Serengeti, Afro-XLMR, AfriBERTA) against global models (LaBSE). Through visualization and error analysis, they traced the gap: African models deeply understand Igbo's linguistic structure but lack internal 'bridges' between Igbo and English representations.
1175.ww: Global models work because they were trained on explicit translation data—seeing the same idea expressed in many language pairs teaches the model to map all languages to a shared underlying space. African-focused models were trained on in-language text, which builds deep understanding but no cross-language bridges. This is a fundamental architectural issue: deep understanding and cross-lingual alignment are different capabilities.
1175.po: The paper reveals the 'Alignment Gap': regional models cannot handle cross-lingual retrieval despite superior language knowledge. This finding reshapes how we should design multilingual systems for low-resource languages: translate-supervised training is essential, not optional. Without this insight, builders might waste effort on more language data when they actually need bridge-building between languages.

1176.bp: When you ask an AI system 'write me a 500-word summary of this research paper', how do you know the answer is any good? You could hire human judges, but that's expensive and slow. Can an LLM itself reliably judge whether another LLM's answer is correct? This question matters because we increasingly rely on AI-generated answers in research and decision-making.
1176.wh: The trap: an LLM asked to judge another LLM's output might favor answers that sound confident or resemble its own style, even if they are factually wrong. It might also favor longer or more complex answers because they feel more thorough. And it might struggle with subtle errors—a citation that looks right but points to the wrong paper, for example. Without ground truth (human judges), you cannot know if the LLM judge is reliable.
1176.ap: Auto-Judge is a benchmark pairing AI-generated answers (from retrieval-augmented generation systems) with human judgments, plus a standardized protocol for testing LLM judges. Researchers submit their own LLM-based judging methods, which are run against the benchmark to see how well they correlate with human ratings. The benchmark includes diagnostic tests for known failure modes: self-preference (favoring its own outputs), circularity (using the answer to verify itself), and manipulation (responding to adversarial inputs).
1176.ww: To improve LLM judges, you must first measure them against ground truth (humans), then stress-test them against tricks and edge cases. This forces researchers to think deeply about how judges can be fooled. Over time, benchmark results accumulate, revealing which judging strategies are robust and which are fragile.
1176.po: The Auto-Judge resource and leaderboard let researchers compare LLM judging methods systematically. It exposes vulnerabilities and validates robust approaches, gradually building a repertoire of trustworthy methods for evaluating AI-generated research summaries and citations—critical infrastructure for AI-assisted science.

1177.bp: When you search for 'best restaurants in Brooklyn under $20', the search engine might suggest 'best restaurants in Brooklyn', 'cheap restaurants near me', or 'date night dining'. These suggestions help you refine your intent. Measuring whether suggestions are good is hard because it depends on what you actually want next—which only you know.
1177.wh: Most systems test suggestions against static lists: 'did the user pick one of our top-5 suggestions?' This ignores the real process: you scan suggestions, dismiss most, and maybe click one that sparks a new direction. Worse, online A/B testing (showing suggestions to real users) is costly, slow, and hard to reproduce for different systems.
1177.ap: SIQSE uses an LLM as a synthetic user that reads suggestions and picks the most contextually relevant one based on its stated search intent. Unlike naive protocols (assume users pick top suggestions), this model simulates actual selective behavior—scanning, filtering, and choosing. The researchers validate this by checking if the model's picks correlate with real human selections across datasets.
1177.ww: By modeling users as thoughtful selectors rather than passive acceptors, SIQSE captures an essential dynamic: good suggestions are not just relevant, they must surprise or clarify your intent. An LLM as synthetic user can express preference based on context, approximating human judgment. The final evaluation metric is not LLM-based—it's a traditional ranking measure—so the result is objective even though the simulation is AI-powered.
1177.po: SIQSE enables reproducible, fast offline evaluation of query suggestion systems that reflects real-world selection behavior. Researchers can now benchmark multiple systems cheaply and repeatedly, accelerating innovation in query suggestions—a crucial feature in modern search where users frequently refine and explore.

1178.bp: Large language models power everything from customer service to medical diagnosis, yet they almost never work in Traditional Mongolian. Without a standard evaluation framework, engineers have no way to know what's broken or whether their fixes actually helped. This problem affects millions of language communities worldwide.
1178.wh: Creating an evaluation benchmark is expensive and requires expertise. For high-resource languages like English, thousands of hours have gone into building benchmarks. For Traditional Mongolian, there's no systematic evaluation infrastructure, so every company or researcher builds ad-hoc tests and findings do not accumulate. Also, simply translating English benchmarks misses language-specific challenges.
1178.ap: TM-Bench combines three construction methods: human-verified translations from English benchmarks, expert-written original tests in Mongolian, and semi-automated synthesis. It covers five tasks (understanding and generation), with 18,357 test instances total. The authors evaluated representative LLMs, using both automatic metrics and double-blind human judging.
1178.ww: By mixing translated, original, and synthesized content, the benchmark covers both universal reasoning skills and language-specific phenomena. The dual evaluation (automatic + human) reveals when a model's scores mislead: low automatic scores might mean the model output is unreadable gibberish (a real problem they found), which human judges can spot.
1178.po: TM-Bench reveals that current models almost fail on Traditional Mongolian understanding tasks and collapse into gibberish on generation. This benchmarks creates shared ground truth, enabling researchers and builders to track progress, compare approaches, and diagnose specific failures—essential infrastructure for building Mongolian-language AI.

1179.bp: Wikipedia is humanity's knowledge platform, but it is editable—and sometimes editors subtly reshape history and cultural attribution. In the Russo-Ukrainian conflict, some editors might gradually shift credit for cultural achievements from Ukraine to Russia, or reframe agency and legitimacy in ways that appear factual but are cumulatively tendentious. Detecting these narratives is crucial for maintaining integrity in shared knowledge.
1179.wh: Misinformation is obvious: a false claim is wrong. Narrative manipulation is insidious: each edit might be defensible individually, yet the accumulation reframes cultural heritage. Detecting this requires comparing sequences of edits, understanding what implicit assumptions change, and distinguishing legitimate rewording from motivated reframing.
1179.ap: The dataset captures paired Wikipedia revisions (before and after edits) in the Russo-Ukrainian context, with editorial history and consistent human annotations showing how cultural attribution and agency shift. Editors labeled specific mechanisms: which cultural elements were credited to which group, how responsibility is framed, what legitimacy is granted.
1179.ww: By examining revision pairs and their context, researchers can train systems to recognize patterns of incremental reframing. A single edit (changing 'Byzantine' to 'Eastern European') seems minor, but patterns of such changes reveal coordination or bias. With labeled pairs, machine learning can generalize to new narratives.
1179.po: The dataset enables systematic study of narrative manipulation—a subtle form of information control that poses new challenges for information retrieval and content moderation. Researchers can develop methods to detect and flag incremental reframing campaigns, protecting shared knowledge platforms from this form of distortion.

1180.bp: Running a shared task (an online competition where researchers submit systems to a common benchmark) is a powerful way to advance research. But conversational search is tricky: systems must interact with simulated users in real-time, and every interaction must be recorded in a standard format. The infrastructure challenges are substantial.
1180.wh: The technical bind: in a typical shared task, you submit a file of results ('run files'). For conversational search, you need live interaction—your system chats with a user simulator, the simulator responds, and the conversation evolves. This means both systems must be online simultaneously, which breaks the file-submission model. Without a clean infrastructure, organizing such shared tasks is a nightmare.
1180.ap: Sim.API is a middleware layer that exposes user simulators as simple web API endpoints and handles recording conversations in a standard format. Researchers' systems call these endpoints (like calling any web API), and the middleware logs every exchange automatically. There's no need for special run files or complex orchestration.
1180.ww: By abstracting the simulator as an API, Sim.API lets each system interact naturally without worrying about the plumbing. The middleware invisibly records everything, so organizers collect uniform, reproducible logs. This turns an infrastructural headache into a straightforward programming task.
1180.po: Sim.API makes it practical for shared-task organizers to include user simulation, and for researchers to develop conversational search systems without custom integration. This accelerates research in conversational AI by lowering the barrier to participation and standardizing how systems are evaluated.

1181.bp: Finding your next apartment requires balancing price, location, and amenities. A good search tool must rank apartments by relevance to *you*—your budget, your commute, your priorities. But real-estate markets are spatially complex (neighborhoods matter enormously) and temporally dynamic (prices shift weekly). Building such ranking systems requires data with rich spatial and temporal signals.
1181.wh: Most ranking datasets are static snapshots. Real-estate is different: a location's value changes over time (a new transit line opens, a neighborhood gentrifies), and comparability depends on geography (a $2M apartment in Manhattan is a different asset class than a $2M apartment in rural Montana). You need a dataset capturing how neighborhoods evolve and how transport accessibility drives price.
1181.ap: RRE-GTC aggregates 456,182 geo-temporal clusters derived from Russian apartment listings, preserving privacy by grouping listings rather than releasing individual addresses. Each cluster contains price dynamics over time (percentile distributions), building stock details, and transport-accessibility signals (proximity to transit, density of transport options). Crucially, the authors derived a 'transport-isolated' price signal via attribution modeling—the price variation explained purely by location versus intrinsic quality.
1181.ww: By clustering and aggregating, RRE-GTC protects privacy while preserving the richness needed for research. The transport-attribution model is clever: it separates two sources of price variation. This lets researchers study whether their ranking system is responding to 'location value' (being near transit) versus 'intrinsic quality' (building condition, amenities)—which would reveal why it's making recommendations.
1181.po: RRE-GTC enables research into geo-temporal ranking (improving apartment search across cities) and market-aware recommendations (systems that understand why prices change). It also supports explainable search—a recommendation can be justified by pointing to specific factors (good transit, recent neighborhood improvement), making the system transparent to users.

1182.bp: Detecting fraud—a criminal using stolen credit cards, a scammer fabricating transactions—is a massive problem for banks. But training fraud-detection systems requires realistic transaction data, which banks guard fiercely due to privacy and competitive concerns. This creates a catch-22: researchers cannot access data to build better detection systems.
1182.wh: Public datasets are too simple or unrealistic: they might show only aggregate fraud rates without capturing real patterns, or they might lack the temporal, relational, and contextual richness of actual banking networks. Oversimplified data leads to systems that work on the benchmark but fail in production.
1182.ap: F2-Gen is an interactive web platform that generates synthetic transaction data and transaction graphs based on parameterized fraud scenarios. Users can configure fraud patterns (e.g., 'small high-frequency purchases from multiple merchants'), visualize the data, and export it. The platform includes automated screening to remove fields that accidentally leak labels, tutorials, baseline scripts, and sanity checks.
1182.ww: By letting researchers configure scenario parameters, F2-Gen bridges the realism gap: simulations can approximate real fraud patterns without revealing actual bank data. The visual exploration and sanity checks ensure the synthetic data is plausible (not obviously broken), and automated screening ensures experiments are not accidentally cheating (using a column that always predicts fraud).
1182.po: Researchers can now generate realistic synthetic transaction data for benchmarking anomaly-detection, graph-learning, and teaching. Because the data is configurable, they can test how systems perform under different fraud regimes—a capability impossible with fixed real datasets. This accelerates research and makes results reproducible and shareable.

1183.bp: You read a book in English, then weeks later you recall a scene but can't remember the exact phrasing: 'What's the word for when someone's on the tip of your tongue?' This 'tip-of-the-tongue' query is hard—you remember context and meaning but not exact wording. Building search systems that handle such fuzzy queries is valuable for retrieval beyond English, where speakers of Chinese, Japanese, or Korean face the same challenge.
1183.wh: Most retrieval benchmarks focus on English and assume clear, well-formed queries. Tip-of-the-tongue queries are vague and describe concepts indirectly, making them much harder. Extending benchmarks to other languages is not trivial: you cannot simply translate English tip-of-the-tongue queries, because what feels fuzzy or context-dependent varies by language and culture.
1183.ap: The researchers built multilingual tip-of-the-tongue benchmarks for Chinese, Japanese, Korean, and English using LLM-based simulation. They systematically tested how the prompt language and the source document language affect the realism of simulated queries, then validated simulated queries by checking if system rankings match rankings from real human tip-of-the-tongue queries.
1183.ww: Simulating tip-of-the-tongue queries requires language-aware prompting. The researchers discovered that using non-English source documents matters—English Wikipedia alone is insufficient because some concepts are better understood in their native cultural context. By validating against real queries, they ensured the simulated queries are realistic, not just plausible-looking.
1183.po: Four new multilingual tip-of-the-tongue benchmarks with 5,000 queries each enable researchers to build and test retrieval systems that handle fuzzy, context-dependent queries in multiple languages. The paper also provides practical guidance on how to construct realistic synthetic queries for under-resourced languages—a recipe applicable far beyond tip-of-the-tongue retrieval.

1184.bp: Building a complete conversational search system requires multiple specialist components: understanding what the user means, ranking candidate results, generating a natural response. Researchers develop new ranking algorithms or response generation techniques, but integrating them into a working end-to-end system is tedious. A modular platform could let each researcher contribute one piece without rebuilding everything.
1184.wh: Conversational search systems are complex: they combine query reformulation, retrieval, ranking, and response generation in a pipeline where outputs of one stage feed into the next. Most researchers code custom systems, making it hard to reuse components and nearly impossible to compare fairly. Existing platforms are either too rigid (no customization) or too bare-bones (everything is a pain).
1184.ap: Orcheo is a modular open-source platform where each component (query reformulation module, ranking module, response generator) is a single-file node. Components expose a standard interface and can be swapped or combined. The platform includes 45+ off-the-shelf modules for common tasks. It supports both prototyping (Python for development) and production deployment (with credentials, telemetry, logging).
1184.ww: Modularity via single-file components lowers the integration cost: a researcher implements a new ranking algorithm in one file, plugging into the standard interface, and it works with any other module. The dual execution mode (prototype vs. production) means researchers can test ideas quickly locally and then deploy to real users with confidence. Built-in AI coding support lowers onboarding friction.
1184.po: Orcheo accelerates conversational search research by cutting implementation time dramatically. Researchers can now focus on their innovation (a better ranking model, a smarter response generator) rather than reinventing infrastructure. The platform also enables fair comparative studies—different research groups use the same base system, differing only in the component under investigation.
